utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber is not informed about any preliminaries, therefore could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I don't seem to be getting sound through my headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you push the volume button several times, then slowly you will start hearing my voice.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you keep speaking, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, just tell me. It's not pushing it, but it's pushing it repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Wilson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Wilson, I'd like to remind you that the solemn declaration you gave yesterday is still binding; that is, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having said this, Ms. Bolton, are you ready to continue your examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Good morning, General Wilson.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I have P326 MFI [sic] up, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: While that's being brought up, General Wilson, you may remember that yesterday the last document we were discussing was the record of the discussions you had with General Mladic and Mrs. Plavsic at Lukavica barracks on the 25th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And I had been asking you some questions yesterday before we looked at that document about the arrangements that had been made for your transportation that day, and you had told me if there had been any firing upon you when you went to the barracks that day that it would have been recorded in the document you created. And having had an opportunity to review the document that's now before you during proofing, was there any record of your having been shot at en route to Lukavica barracks on the 25th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't re-read the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'll leave that issue then for now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 20799A, please. For the record, this is a document that's discussed at paragraph 75 of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I'm just waiting for the document to be brought up in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I meanwhile take the opportunity to -- well, I don't know who I'm correcting. But P326 is admitted into evidence. It's not MFI'd. I'm referring to page 2, line 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Before you, General Wilson, you should see a transcript of an intercepted conversation dated the 25th of May, 1992, where the speakers have been identified as Ratko Mladic and an unidentified male.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if you would look part-way down the page you would notice that there is a quotation from General Mladic which reads as follows: "Be stubborn, observe, and make sure your men have had a good rest. Put observers. If a single bullet is fired at you or at 'Jusuf Dzonlic' barracks or 'Marsal Tito' barracks or if a single soldier is wounded either at the front or in the barracks, I will retaliate against the town." The other male replies: "Yes, sir." General Mladic states: "Make sure that your soldiers are aware that Sarajevo is going to shake." The other male says: "Okay." And General Mladic is saying: "Sarajevo will shake, more shells will fall on per second than in the entire war so far." Can you tell me how the position that General Mladic is quoted as taking in this intercept on the 25th of May, 1992, compares with the position he took during the meeting with you and Mrs. Plavsic that same day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it accurately reflects the statements that he made at our meeting on the same day. He was showing some determination to carry out such action unless the barracks were evacuated safely.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can I have page 2 of this document, please, in both English and B/C/S. And if we could scroll down in the -- in both pages, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: At the very bottom of the second page in English General Mladic is quoted as saying: "We have the means and the bridges with which to cross the river. I have blocked Sarajevo from four corners. The city is trapped. There is no way out." How does that statement correspond with the actual state of affairs on the 25th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reality is on the 25th of May, the city was fully invested by the Serb forces and it was virtually impossible to move in or out of the city. Now, that statement there reflects the reality on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that be introduced as the next exhibit MFI, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours 65 ter 20799A will be P327 marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And keeps that status for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that the second barracks to be evacuated in Sarajevo was the Jusuf Dzonlic barracks. Do you have any recollection of the date or the approximate date when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it took place on the 27th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And could you tell us whether that evacuation went smoothly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was an absolute disaster.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What went wrong?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sides had been negotiating all day -- in fact, some of those negotiations were taking place down at the Presidency. They arrived back at the PTT building quite late in the day at about 4.30 and announced that it had been agreed the evacuation could take place. There was no plan. The barracks commander hadn't really been warned that the barracks were about to be evacuated. It all seemed rushed and confused. I counselled both sides at the time, saying it would be better to wait until the next day, and they were determined that it should take place. So at about 1800, I think, or 6.00 in the evening they went to the barracks and started to get things organised there and it was mass confusion. Trucks had been preloaded with weapons that it was agreed should be left behind, some of the BH militias got into the barracks and were searching the vehicles and were looting. The soldiers and a limited number of civilians were unaware of what was required. Once again, at about 8.00 at night I warned the parties a potential disaster existed and that they should rethink the plan to evacuate the building that night. They were determined to continued. Eventually at about 8.30 and in dark they left the barracks, some 150-odd vehicles. The lead vehicle which was or which contained Colonel Cadjo took a wrong turn. Colonel Cadjo thought that the agreed route would be ambushed as it happened in the very first barracks evacuation. So he changed the route with General Boskovic's approval, but none of the militias on the ground knew that they were coming so eventually they bumped into a number of different militia positions. Firing took place. The convoy broke up. At least one soldier was killed in the firing, a number were wounded. The vehicles were scattered all over Sarajevo. Some vehicles got out successfully to Lukavica. About 30 vehicles lost the next day and about 30 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 10733, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, what role did General Boskovic play in evacuating that barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Boskovic was the senior JNA negotiator, and he was the actual overall co-ordinator for the JNA during the evacuation. He was supervising the evacuation. He travelled in the last vehicle out of the barracks. Colonel Cadjo was in the first vehicle out of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And before you, you have -- you should see a document. Could you tell us who authored this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. It's a lieutenant-colonel. It might be one of the staff officers in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could we turn to page 2 in both English and B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document that's now before you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. It's a record of a meeting held in the afternoon on the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, the date on the top of the page is the 28th of May. Does that correspond with your recollection or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, it's the 28th of May, the day after the evacuation of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And were you present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: General Boskovic is quoted on the page before us as saying: "I'd like to say what happened yesterday. I was with Cadjo, and as the agreement wasn't respected from the Serbian side Cadjo and I went to the Presidency." He goes on to explain later on that page that, at the very bottom: "We had a definite route. Some people couldn't believe that they were sure so they changed the route."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you could please turn to the next page in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The top of the page he goes on to say: "The convoy was broken on Stup's loop. We were attacked by Serbian Territorial Defence (SDT) and Territorial Defence (TOBH) ..." And he goes on to say if these soldiers were wounded and one was killed. Does that correspond with your recollection of events?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that be marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the exhibit, Ms. Bolton, I see text in the English version which is not English but appears in B/C/S, isn't it? First page -- the first page where you started.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we go back to the first page. Unless you could tell me what "werkexemplaar" means. You are using it, and apparently I take it that you understand what the content is. It is translated, so the parties -- it's Dutch. Please look at it for me at this moment and I'm consulting with my colleagues. There's no reason not to admit it. But please take care that you don't have third languages in your documents. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours 65 ter 10733 shall be assigned Exhibit P328. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. One of the reasons, by the way, Ms. Bolton why I'm even mentioning it is because there's text under it which I have difficulties in finding in the original, as a matter of fact. That is the line in the original with starts with "broj stranice," and I have no idea whether it corresponds with the original language. Is it an explanation of the Dutch language? Is it -- I have no idea, but it's -- certainly needs some additional attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll check the translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please. Then I still have to decide on admission. P328 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. So, General Wilson, we've been discussing then an intercept where General Mladic is quoted as making some threats about making Sarajevo shake, and you've told us about some threats that were made at a meeting that you had with him, that if the barracks weren't evacuated within three days that certain things would happen. Was the Marsal Tito barracks evacuated by the 28th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was there shelling the night of the 28th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you please describe its intensity for us?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It, once again, was -- it was probably the biggest night of shelling of the city from April, and it started I think in the evening at about 1700, went through until early morning. It appeared that the whole city was being engaged, not just particular areas, but there was an emphasis of fire down in the old city, down in the city centre. And there were literally thousands of rounds of all calibres, including rocket-launchers, being fired into the city and distributed in such a way that there appeared to be no particular targets involved, just a general engagement of the city. And it was certainly -- it was the second-biggest night I remember of my time down there of the shelling. It was -- it was a really horrendous experience for the inhabitants of Sarajevo on that particular night.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Where was the -- where were the shells falling relative to the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There appeared to be no relationship between the shelling and the confrontation line. The city itself was the target. There was a lot of firing around the PTT, but the weight of fire seemed to be going into the old city.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 09964, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You should see a document before you. There's a signature on the top of the document. Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And His Honour was asking a question earlier about the fact that the work "werkexemplaar" appears to have been placed on the document at some point. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a Dutch signals company providing communications for us from Sarajevo to the rest of the world. It may well be a security classification or a priority of handling. I don't speak Dutch, so I don't know, but it was stamped on there by a Dutch signaller.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And this document subject matter is: "Record of conversation with BiH and JNA delegations 29th May, 1992." Could you tell us who authored the document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I authored the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: At paragraph 76 of your statement you refer to a meeting you attended on the 29th of May, 1992, with General Boskovic, Colonel Cadjo, and Lieutenant-Colonel Jankovic. Is this the meeting you were referring to at that part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you tell us what General Boskovic had to say about the attack the previous night?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Boskovic and, indeed, Colonel Cadjo also wished to dissociate themselves with the attack that was launched upon the city the night before. They recognised the gravity and the severity of the attack. They indicated they thought General Mladic was out of control, that pressure had been put on him by JNA authorities to stop the attack, and that he had ignored that approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but could we on our screens go back to the document rather than to the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Boskovic actually apologised on behalf of the JNA for the conduct of General Mladic and he certainly wanted to have nothing to do with any responsibility for the attack on that night.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Now, the first -- the meeting apparently according to paragraph 1 started at 8.00 a.m. and there's an indication there as to who was present at that time. Were you later joined by other participants?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was in the afternoon that the representatives of the Presidency arrived, led by Mr. Doko.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could we have page 2 of this document, please. And if we could concentrate on paragraph 5 in particular. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us, sir, what occurred when the general -- sorry, not general, Minister Doko and the other representatives from the Presidency attended?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they brought a tape with them that they said the group would be very interested in listening to. They subsequently played that tape. It was a recording of General Mladic giving artillery fire commands and orders on the night of the 28th, and you could -- it was given in -- the tape and recording was done in Bosnian -- in Serbo-Croat, which I don't -- or in Serb which I don't speak, so Colonel Cadjo translated for me. And he said that General Mladic was directing fire at individual target areas. He was ordering fire at his command; that means that you can't fire unless he says so and you fire when he says so. And he was orchestrating the calibres of fire that were being used from time to time during the attack. I must say that the group was somewhat dismayed collectively at the contents of the tape, and there was much shaking of heads and dismay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can I ask you what General Boskovic's reaction was to the tape?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, firstly he certainly thought it was General Mladic. He recognised the voice as did Colonel Cadjo. And they, once again, wished to dissociate themselves with the attack that was launched on the city that night. He apologised for General Mladic's behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Although you don't speak Serbian, did you recognise any voices on the recording?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't say I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And you indicated that Colonel Cadjo was providing some translation to you. In paragraph 5, halfway through, we have an indication starts with: "The tape showed that General Mladic personally directed the artillery attack on the city" and it says "(English transcript to be provide). He selected targets including the Presidency, town hall, police headquarters and children's embassy and directed fire away from Serb populated areas. Fire was at his direct command and he directed the cease-fire of light calibre weapons to allow 155 MM artillery and multiple rocket launchers to engage targets." The information there about what was being targeted, what areas were being targeted and what buildings were being targeted, where did that information come from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That came from Colonel Cadjo's translation, his oral translation. I can't recall what happened to the written translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that document be admitted as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number would be ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 09964 shall be assigned Exhibit P329.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P329 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I please have 65 ter 22234. Sorry, there should be an English translation as well. The Court's indulgence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You should now see before you, General Wilson, a series of transcripts from intercepted conversations, and I'm only going to ask you about a few of them. The first is conversation 15 which appears starting at the bottom of page 1, and I'm just going to ask you if you would read that conversation to yourself. And when you're at the bottom of the page, please let the court clerk know and he'll change or he'll turn the page for you electronically.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There appears to be orders to fire at two neighbourhoods in Sarajevo, Velesici and Bascarsija. And my question is: As a member of the Australian army, when you receive or issue orders to fire how specifically is the actual target identified in the orders?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The target is identified by a map reference, either a six-figure or an eight-figure number which allows you to identify on the ground to an accuracy of either a hundred metres or 10 metres, a hundred metres being the maximum that you would ever give to an artillery unit to fire. So you're being quite precise about where you want the rounds to land.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, although the witness is well into his answer, my objection would be: Is he talking now about facts concerning the shelling of Velesici or is he speaking from the area of his expertise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, he's telling facts he knows about his own background; that is, how these matters are done in the Australian army, how orders would be given there and would be received there. That's what I understand the testimony is about. And those are facts, I take it. It's not expert opinion about whether it's good what they do in Australia or whether it's better what they do in Sarajevo. Yes, again apparently the objection has been withdrawn. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what is the benefit of targeting or pin-pointing a target with that degree of precision?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're maximising the opportunity for accuracy and minimising the danger of rounds landing where you don't want them to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you explain what area fire is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time in a military operation you may wish to engage an area as opposed to a specific target. It might be to keep the enemy's head down while you're manoeuvring. It might be to inflict damage upon a particular area. So from time to time, it is normal to engage an area, but for economy of fire the normal practice is to be as accurate as you can with what is essentially an area weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And have you ever issued an order for area fire in an urban environment?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there is a great danger of collateral damage and of civilian casualties, that in urban areas the emphasis is on achieving the greatest accuracy you can and your selection of weapons is to ensure that that accuracy is achieved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Wilson, could I ask you: Have you ever been in a situation where you were engaged in combat close to an urban environment, where you were one of the parties to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a -- close to a village -- well, that's not quite urban, but a rural village, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was wondering whether you were telling us at this moment what you should do or what you had done and why you didn't do it. Were you ever at a point that you were considering to fire into an urban or a village area and then refrained from doing it for the reasons you gave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've been questioned about doctrine under which I was educated, and that's what I'm really responding to rather than experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, this of course comes close to expert evidence, Ms. Bolton, and although you introduced the matter by what -- whether this witness had ever done something, but it slipped into opinion rather than that it stayed with the facts you were starting with.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Right. And to the extent that it has, Your Honour, my respectful submission would be that the jurisprudence of this Tribunal has permitted persons with military expertise to express opinions on matters of this nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You didn't hear me say that it was totally inadmissible. What you heard me say is that you slipped from facts to something else, and it became unclear whether the witness was testifying about his experience or about his knowledge on a theoretical level and that's what I wanted to be put clearly on the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And do you need me to explore that any further or is it clear to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We leave it to you, but we would have no further need for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please have page 3 in both English and B/C/S in this document. And we'll be looking at conversation 3 which is at the bottom of both pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And again, if you could read the conversation and let the clerk know when to turn the page for you, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which conversation, 3?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Conversation 3, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Approximately halfway down the page - we're on page 4 now - you'll see there's a quote to: "Fire at Velesici and at Pofalici where there aren't many Serb inhabitants ." And I believe the number 1 is ascribed to General Mladic. How does that compare with what you were told by Colonel Cadjo was on the recording that you listened to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It confirms that General Mladic was identifying specific targets to be attacked on the night of the 28th of May. He was personally identifying specific areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What about the reference to "where there aren't many Serb inhabitants." Do you recall whether that was something that Colonel Cadjo told you about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I have the -- could we scroll down the same page, please, look at conversation 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And here I just have some questions. There's a reference at line 3 to 155's and multiple rocket launchers. What are 155's?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: 155 is a medium artillery piece that has a range of about 30 kilometres and has a very large explosion when it lands. If it were to hit a normal suburban concrete house, it would completely destroy it. Rocket launchers fire multiple rockets, perhaps 30 at a time. They're an area weapon. They're about 120-millimetre calibre. When they land, they land as a group and have quite an impressive explosive effect upon the ground. Once again, they'd be highly destructive in an urban area.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in your view appropriate to use in an urban environment where there's civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe they have the accuracy one would be seeking in an urban area.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Finally, could we have page 5 in English and 5 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I think the entirety of the conversation is visible on page 5 in the B/C/S, but in the English you're going to have to read conversation 12 and then let, again, the clerk know when you've finished that page and when he can turn the page for you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could we just go back to page 5 in English, please. Now, in this conversation, General Wilson, there is a reference by one of the gentlemen to the runway. Could you tell us whether there were Bosnian Serb forces in proximity to the airport at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time the Bosnian Serb forces controlled the Sarajevo airport.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And at the very beginning of the conversation the two speakers are talking about multiple rocket launchers firing and 155's, and then Private Cekovic refers to comets, "those comets, you know, comets flashing on all sides." What do you take that to be a reference to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he's referring to the multiple rocket launchers. They leave a trail of fire behind them as they move through the air.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And there's also an indication approximately two-thirds of the way down the page that the fire went on -- he says "we caused" -- I'm looking at speaker number 1: "It seems we caused bedlam. We caused -- you have no idea how long the fire went on for, until 2.00 or 3.00." Does that correspond with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There's also a reference further down the page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There is again Private Cekovic quoted as saying part-way through the paragraph: "You should have seen the chaos, fuck it, how they fired at them with Pragas, how they fired at them. It was chaos." What is a Pragas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what a Pragas is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you tell me what the destructive fire is of an anti-aircraft gun?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when it's employed in a ground role, it has a high volume of fire. It fires typically an explosive round varying between 20 and 40 millimetres. And because it has such a rapid rate of fire and an explosive effect at the other end, it can just tear buildings apart in a very short period of time. It's a very impressive weapon when used in the ground role.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted, please, as the next exhibit marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The number would be, Mr. Registrar ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours 65 ter 22234 will be P330 marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. Could we please bring up Exhibit P00072 which is part of 65 ter I think 22460 and -- the Court's indulgence. I'm sorry -- no, that's fine. And I think it's -- is there a sub (C) under that exhibit? If so, that's what we will want.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In the meantime, I will ask General Wilson, in terms of the artillery fire that you described from the evening of May 28th into May 29th, could you tell us what kind of preparations you would have to take before launching a barrage of this nature?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly you would require the ammunition to be there and you would need to pre-plan that. There was a vast quantity of ammunition consumed on that night that would have require some planning to preposition that ammunition. I doubt that they would have that sort of on the gun-line on a routine basis. And then of course if one is being serious about accuracy, one would pre-register targets. You actually trial firing a few rounds so that you know exactly where they will land and you've got the right data in your gun position so that when they actually fire the target on the night it will be accurate. Following that you would fire what is called an on-call target, I believe it is, where you just fire into the general area and then adjust your fire as you're going. But ideally you would have all your targets pre-registered and ready to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm going to play you a short clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I can tell the Court that we're not relying on the audio at all for the clip. It's just the images that we'll be asking the witness to comment on. And the timing is from 14 to 32 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you do not rely on the text, may I take it that you also do not want to tender the text in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I do not wish to tender the text in transcript. I think it's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's the case, then of course you will understand that I don't have a recollection of every single piece of evidence at this moment. Please proceed. The video needs to be played only once.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us how the explosions and the fire -- artillery fire that we saw in that clip compared to what you observed on the 28th/29th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about 30 seconds of what went on in the city all night and generally distributed around the city. What we could see there were tracer bullets moving through the air. It's just a snap-shot of a very small part of the city, but does reflect the intensity that was going on really for hours and hours at a time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could we now have Exhibit D00039, please, and I would be asking for page 5 in both -- sorry, first page 1 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Once again, the interpreters are kindly requesting the parties to please slow down and the witness to wait before he answers - thank you very much - a little bit. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Wilson, you've heard the request to take a short break between the question and answer. And Ms. Bolton will do the same between answer and question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: All right, you should see before you now, General Wilson, a conversation between Ratko Mladic and Potpara that is indicated was intercepted on the 29th May, 1992. And could I now have page 5 in both English and B/C/S, please. Sorry, I had the wrong page number in B/C/S. It's page 4. And if we could scroll down to the bottom of the page in both versions. You see very near to the bottom of the page, General Wilson, that General Mladic is quoted as saying: "I agree. I want the same thing. If they want peace, they can have it. I ordered yesterday evening as soon as I arrived, there was that attack not only against the units but also against you. This shooting, somehow I managed to calm down the men here, to get them under control, to stop them from firing. This thing they are doing now, they probably have good pantomimes or some good impressionists who probably successfully imitated our voices, mine, yours, everybody's." May I ask you what your response would be to a suggestion that the voice on the radio intercepts that you were played during your meeting with the Presidency was the voice of a mimic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that the six officers from the JNA and the Presidency who were there had no doubt that the voice in that tape belonged to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask, please, to go back to page 1 in both versions of this document, please. And could you scroll down in the English version and the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The very last entry from Ratko Mladic on that page starts with saying: "... for you to know. First of all, they are listening in on our conversations ..." Who do you understand he would be talking about when he says "they are listening in"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he's referring to the Presidency military forces, to their radio intercept people.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I now have 65 ter 09967.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask you while that document's coming up, what was the Secretary-General of the United Nations reaction to the bombardment of Sarajevo on May 28th/29th?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He issued a call for the Serb parties to show restraint and ask that representations be made to the Serb authorities to call for that restraint. And I was asked by the force commander, General Nambiar, to arrange a meeting with the local Serb political and military leadership to pass the Secretary-General's concern and call for a restrain on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And do you recognise the document that's before you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And that appears to be a press release issued by the Secretary-General relating to the bombardment?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that be marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 09967 will be Exhibit P331. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 11321, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: While that's coming up, you indicated that you received a plea of sorts from the Secretary-General to call for restraint and you were asked to arrange for a meeting. Did you, in fact, meet with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I met with General Mladic and Mrs. Plavsic on the 30th of May at Lukavica barracks. I passed on the appeal and the concern of the Secretary-General at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document that is before you, General Wilson?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, it's a cable authored and signed by me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when you met with General Mladic on the 30th of May, 1992, did he deny that his forces were responsible for the bombardment the evening before?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did he acknowledge that they were responsible?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did and his justification was that the standard justification that that was simply defending the Serb people and Serb neighbourhoods in Sarajevo from attack from the Presidency forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Had you seen signs that there was an all-out attack by Presidency forces throughout the city of Sarajevo on the 28th and 29th that they would have needed to repel against?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- it was pretty much one-way traffic. I -- of course because of the volume of fire that was going on that night, it was virtually impossible to hear any outgoing fire, but if it was it would have been minimal in comparison to the incoming fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And at any point during your meeting with General Mladic on the 30th of May, 1992, did he suggest that there was some false propaganda out there in terms of there being somebody mimicking him on an alleged intercept?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that point was never raised on the 30th of May nor at any other time by General Mladic with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that be marked as the next exhibit, Your Honour, and that would be a convenient place for the morning break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 11321 will be Exhibit P332. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P332 is admitted into evidence. Ms. Bolton, could you give us a time estimate on how much time you would still need.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: 20 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll verify how much time you used until now. I expect that 20 minutes would just keep you within the time estimate you gave at the beginning. We first would like to have Mr. -- the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom, Mr. Wilson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break of 20 minutes and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, please proceed. You have 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May we have 65 ter 09966.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, General Wilson, when I was questioning you earlier about Defence Exhibit 39 which was the intercept where General Mladic was referring to pantomimes or mimics, in that intercept I read you a portion about where he indicated that they may be listening or they are listening to our conversations. Do you have any knowledge about whether in May of 1992 the opposing forces were able to listen to one another's conversations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know definitively, but any soldier on operations would expect that the opposing side is monitoring your communications. That's normal practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you have before you a document dated 30th May 1992, which is a summary of a meeting with President Milosevic. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I've seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And were you in attendance at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were you briefed as to what occurred at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was. When Mr. Cedric Thornberry, the chief civil affairs officer, arrived in Sarajevo on the 2nd of June for the airport negotiations, he briefed me on this meeting and other meetings which had taken place which were a preamble to our negotiations on the opening of the airport.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And do you remember very briefly what Mr. Thornberry told you was President Milosevic's position with respect to the bombardment on the 28th/29th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In short he in no way supported or condoned it and thought that General Mladic had grossly misbehaved.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And does the contents of this document accord with the briefing you received from Mr. Thornberry?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that be introduced as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your speed of speech, again, Ms. Bolton, was causing some problems. Yes, the next exhibit -- no, I was focusing on the -- on listening to the other channels in order to find out whether the interpretation was able to keep up. Therefore, I -- my attention was distracted for a second. Mr. Registrar, the number would be ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 09966 will be Exhibit P333. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P333 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Now, I understand from your statement, General Wilson, and this is -- no need to go to it, but at paragraphs 84 to 92, that you were involved in negotiations surrounding the opening of the Sarajevo airport in early June 1992. Could you tell us when relative to those negotiations -- first of all, do you recall the date when those or dates when those negotiations took place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The negotiations started on the 2nd of June when Mr. Thornberry arrived from Belgrade and concluded with the signing of the agreement on the 5th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when relative to those negotiations did the evacuation of the Marsal Tito barracks take place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marsal Tito barracks were evacuated during the negotiations. The exact date I don't recall, but it was either the 3rd or 4th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And I think you've answered this already, what was the state of artillery fire into Sarajevo during those evacuations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was absolute quiet in the city for the first time in many days on the day that the Tito barracks were evacuated because both sides wanted the cease-fire to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And who agreed to the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb political leadership and the Presidency political leadership signed -- I'm sorry, the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA were the lead negotiators; that's General Boskovic, and the BiH military representatives, Mr. Doko may have been replaced by then. I'm just not exactly sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And so who was it that indicated there wouldn't be artillery fire during the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the parties agreed to that requirement, and in particular the JNA and I assume with the agreement of General Mladic who ultimately controlled artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how did the evacuation of that barracks proceed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very smoothly and without hiccup.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And once the evacuation was complete and the troops were safely out of the barracks, what happened to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The night that the -- the night of the evacuation, Serb artillery engaged the barracks with white phosphorus incendiary ammunition and basically burnt the barracks down with any of the contents that may have remained at that time, including at least some of the heavy weapons that were left behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And can you describe how accurate or inaccurate the fire was by the Serb artillery in respect of engaging the barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very accurate and very effective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No comments, no loud speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And after in the days following, was there any improvement in terms of what you have previously described as periods of heavy sustained shelling of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after the signing of the airport agreement on the 5th of June, heavy fighting resumed within the city, in particular around the airport and the Dobrinja area and later around Grbavica, I think it's pronounced, which is adjacent to the Marsal Tito barracks. There was extremely heavy fighting took place then for a period of about seven days and basically continued until I left the city on the 23rd of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 09380, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could I ask one question. You said the shelling of the Marsal Tito barracks was very accurate, very, very precise. Now, it is my understanding that barracks, including the Marsal Tito barracks, cover a certain area which is more than one -- the size of one or two houses but is really a complex of buildings perhaps with some yards. Now, what did you mean exactly by the accuracy? Was it that they didn't hit the yard but only the buildings -- or, I mean to say it was very accurate? But if it's, well, let's say a complex say the size of hundreds of metres, then how could you assess the accuracy of the artillery attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The barracks was too far from the PTT for me to actually observe the fire that night, and in any event we wouldn't be out wandering around the city at night under the conditions that existed at that time. But I did see the barracks in the couple of days afterwards and I'm assessing that something like 80 per cent, 70, 80 per cent of all the buildings were completely burnt out. But the area around had suffered very little collateral damage and that's why I say it was accurate and effective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, there had been shelling all over the city in the days before, isn't it? You said the damage was little in terms of fire or how should I understand you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can see that buildings are shattered, broken. Roofs have been removed, holes blown in walls, litter about the place and area that has been attacked. Now, this area was not subjected to artillery fire while the JNA were in there because the Serb forces would have been concerned about collateral damage that may have been caused to the barracks while they were still occupied. So prior to the evacuation there was not a great deal of artillery directed in that area. A day or two after the evacuation where there was no longer this concern, there was little damage to the buildings in the area of the barracks, so the fire that had produced the destruction of the barracks had to have been accurate and basically confined largely to the area of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, could I just try to imagine what has happened and I now take a scenario which may be unrealistic, but then please tell me. You fire a couple of incendiary projectiles on the barracks, the fire spreads among the buildings but is limited to the barracks because the distance to the adjacent construction outside the barracks is too big for the fire to spread over there. Now, I know that this is -- let me see why is my explanation of the situation not correct and why is your explanation, which is a conclusion on the basis of what you've seen the days after, why is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you'll forgive me, it's 20 years ago so I only have in my mind now an impression that the barracks were surrounded by an open area, that there were not civilian buildings close up to the barracks, that there was some distance. So a fire in the barracks, in my recollection, is unlikely to have spread outside --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- to other areas. So your description is accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that is a possible explanation, apart from the accuracy of the firing you just adopted as an explanation for the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But as I say, I could not observe any damage to the buildings around from artillery or any significant damage in comparison to the rest of the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not blaming you for what you could see or could not see. What I'm trying to do is to see to what extent I can follow your conclusions as compelling conclusions on the basis of what you'd seen the day after. And you say: Well, my scenario, to say so, could not be excluded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Part of the scenario that His Honour just put to you was the suggestion that the fire damage that you saw to 70 or 80 per cent of the buildings within the barracks compound could have been the result of one or two shells. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. It's more likely that there were multiple incendiary rounds fired into the barracks to make sure the job was correctly done. But as I've indicated, we were not in a position to observe the fire, only the effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I don't know if you can answer this question 20 years later, but do you recall how -- what the spacing was like in between buildings within the barracks compound at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, you should now have in front of you 09380, which is -- sorry, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a copy of the agreement signed by both the BH Presidency and the -- and Mr. Karadzic for the opening of the Sarajevo airport.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if you look at paragraph 2 there is a reference to all anti-aircraft weapons systems being withdrawn, and in subparagraph (B) to systems being placed in concentrated areas agreed by UNPROFOR and subject to UNPROFOR observation. Yesterday you gave evidence about concentration areas for Serb weaponry. Is this what you were referring to or is this something different?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the final page in both B/C/S and in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You'll see that there's a signature and you told us this was an agreement agreed to by both the Presidency and the Serb side, and I see only Mr. Karadzic's signature; why is that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because during 1992 and 1993, to my knowledge at least, the Bosnian Presidency refused to meet with the Serb political leadership, nor to sign any documents that they had physically signed. So it was necessary to have shuttle diplomacy between the two parties in different rooms or different physical locations. And when documents were presented, to have two copies, one for each party to sign.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that be introduced as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours 65 ter 09380 will be Exhibit P334. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 19595, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And I'm just going to change to the last subject matter I'm going to ask you about, General Wilson, which is the issue of detention facilities and allegations of ethnic cleansing. At paragraphs 94 and 95 of your statement you indicate that you started to receive reports of ethnic cleansing commencing in March and April of 1992. Could you tell us in what areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina those reported activities were allegedly occurring?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- there was a belt across northern Bosnia just south of the Sava River, but basically from Bihac right across to the Serbian border and also in Drina valley. They were the main areas that we were receiving reports about alleged ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what persons were being ethnically cleansed according to the reports you were receiving?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time the reports that we were receiving were only Muslim people were being moved on, although later I was aware that really all three nationalities suffered the same treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And could you tell us what the sources of your information were about the ethnic cleansing of the Muslim population in the areas you've referred to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily through the media but authoritatively through the ECMM who were responsible for monitoring that type of activity and who exchanged with us on a regular basis information and reports. We were quite well informed about their activities and about their reporting.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And you should see before you a document 19595. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a letter from the Presidency to me highlighting concern about ethnic cleansing which had taken place I think in the Prijedor area.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Now, according to your statement, you had the opportunity to visit area of Bijeljina, and at paragraph 97 you also include some observations of paramilitary forces, including Arkan's men and the White Eagles. And your observation was that the paramilitaries seem to enjoy freedom of movement. Were the paramilitary forces armed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones that I physically saw were armed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in areas controlled by what forces or entities did the paramilitaries seem to enjoy freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them specifically in Knin, in the Krajina, and also in eastern Slavonia in the area of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And who controlled those areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb political authorities controlled those from a political point of view, and Mr. -- General Mladic, at least in the area of Knin, had been able to demonstrate his military authority in those areas also.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You also discuss at paragraph 101 of your statement allegations that the Bosnian Serb forces were engaging in a large-scale detention of civilians, and you indicate that you raised this issue at airport talks. And you record in your statement Mrs. Plavsic's reaction. Could you tell us whether General Mladic participated in the airport talks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was present during the negotiations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you recall, if at all, his reaction to this issue?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: On those occasions, no. He was certainly present and heard the conversations, but they were directed to Mrs. Plavsic. She represented herself as having some responsibility for humanitarian affairs in the Serbian political leadership.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what about the issue of allegations of ethnic cleansing, was that brought up at all in the airport talks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall. They were very focused on opening the airport, trying to keep all the distractions out of there as possible. It was complicated and difficult enough without introducing other subjects.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in your statement you indicate at paragraphs 101 and 113 that General Mladic sometimes attended meetings - and now this would be later in time - of the ICFY and that Lord Owen frequently raised the issue of claims of ethnic cleansing, POWs, and detention centres in those meetings. Do you have any recollection of General Mladic's reaction to any of those discussions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't link General Mladic to any warning or discussion involving Lord Owen and ethnic cleansing. He may or may not have been present. I can't say he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I have this document marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 19595 will be Exhibit P335. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And, finally, could I have Exhibit P00205, which is a video, and the timing I'm going to be playing in a moment - again, we don't rely on the audio - will be 6 minutes and 42 seconds to 6 minutes and 49 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And while that's being brought up, General, I'm going to remind you that at paragraph 104 of your statement you gave evidence about discussing a famous photograph of a man in a detention camp with General Mladic. Do you recall that conversation with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask that we play this little bit of footage, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Will you stop, please. So we played from 6.42 to 6.47.5 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There is an image of a gentleman that is now before you. Could you tell me anything about this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a photograph that was circulating in the media during 1992 and was alleged to have been taken of inmates of a concentration -- of a -- yes, a concentration camp which was being run by the Serbs to hold prisoners. And the -- it was -- the media reports associated with this photograph suggested that this was -- this individual was showing signs of the sort of treatment that was dealt out to the inmates of those camps.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And is this an image of the gentleman that you refer to in paragraph 104 of your statement or was that a different photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's the same photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm finished with that document and that brings me to the end of my examination-in-chief except for the issue of the associated exhibits that have not been discussed with the witness. Would you like me to discuss that issue now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's best to do that now so the Defence knows during cross-examination where we stand.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I can indicate that of the exhibits there are, I believe, eight associated exhibits that I didn't have the opportunity to discuss with the witness. Two of those the Prosecution isn't seeking to introduce. So the Prosecution is not seeking to introduce 65 ter 10580 or 11095, as I believe the evidence the witness has given in court plus his statement accurately covers the subject matter. And I am seeking to introduce as associated exhibits the remaining 65 ter numbers, which are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would call them one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Receives, Mr. Registrar, number ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P336, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next one, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, 03707.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Receives number ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P337, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Receives number ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P338, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Receives number ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P339, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Receives number ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P340, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Receives number ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And Ms. Stewart's records and mine don't accord with respect to Exhibit 03281. I thought I discussed that with the witness and it was already introduced. Could ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is UNPROFOR cable, summary of meeting between McKenzie, Morillon, and Auger dated 30th of May. I will consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I just have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, if that could be given an exhibit number, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours 65 ter 03281 will be Exhibit P342. And for the clarification of transcript, 65 ter 10789 will be Exhibit P341. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber, Ms. Bolton, has considered that the number of associated exhibits which should be limited, the Chamber accepts the number of seven associated exhibits. P336 up to and including P342 are admitted into evidence. Mr. Petrusic, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Wilson?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Defence is ready to begin with our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon -- good morning, General. Sir, I would like to begin with where you left off, or rather, where the Prosecutor left off with the examination-in-chief. You were shown a photograph and I won't really deal with that, but I would like to ask you this: Do you have any information as to what these people looked like, the people shown in this photograph before they entered the camp?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And just an additional question to deal with that: Do you know whether this photograph of these people, these men, was made from inside the camp or from outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, in paragraph 16 you talk about your mission upon your arrival in Yugoslavia, in Belgrade, Zagreb, and then in Sarajevo, and you say that at this time Mr. Thornberry had a leading role and General Nambiar to a lesser extent. You say also that at the time you were just an actor in the organisational sense. Now, would you agree with me that irrespective of this position that you state in this paragraph, during your stay there in the first ten months you've actually held a number -- a large number of meetings and had numerous contacts with the two primary warring parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- yes, counsellor, that's a true summary of my total time there. But that paragraph is really talking about the period from 22 March until 16 or 17 May, when other people were more involved in the more significant negotiations and I was a relatively junior commander and staff officer, in that period, March to mid-May.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: After mid-May you had under your command - if I may put it that way - a number of observers, UN observers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Their job - as the name itself indicates - was to compile all kinds of information relating to any developments within the warring parties. Is that correctly -- would that be right to say?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsellor, that was one of their jobs. They had many other roles and functions, but actually recording information and reporting it was one of their more important roles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If we can focus just on the information that they gathered relating to whatever was happening on either side of the warring parties, no doubt they would have reported on that; right? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a very general question. They submitted regular reports on what was happening in their area of interest, and they would submit specific reports about individual actions or investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, your reports, were they drafted also based on the information that you received from these observers when they were submitting their reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes that's correct; sometimes my reports were based upon my own experience and observations. It depends on the circumstances, counsellor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You also talk in your statement about meetings that you had with representatives of UNPROFOR. The information that you received from -- or, rather, you and UNPROFOR representatives, did you exchange information between the two of you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was quite a sophisticated system of reporting and exchange of information that existed within UNPROFOR. And I was fortunate enough to be included in the most critical committees and meetings. So I was very well informed about what was happening within UNPROFOR in 1992 and then later in 1993 when I was in Geneva. I had access to the most sensitive information within UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The information that you had access to also had to do with the events in Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but Sarajevo was only one area of interest for UNPROFOR. There were many other areas also.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 38 you mention that you were absent between the 30th of April and the 13th of May, 1992, from the area. Now, would you agree with me that after your return you were briefed on the developments and the events that had happened in Sarajevo, at least the key events, the key developments, that transpired while you were away?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a very short briefing from General McKenzie, who on the 15th of May when this briefing took place, perhaps it was on the 16th of May, he had many other distractions and concerns so the briefing was confined to essentials and not very detailed. But my staff who - that's the military observers - did brief me in a bit more detail, but they were not knowledgeable about the evacuation of the first JNA barracks. So that's a hole in my information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So, General, sir, you're trying to say that you had no information whatsoever about an attack on a column of privates and officers that was withdrawing under the agreement from the command of the 2nd Military District, and this happened on the 3rd of May when this column was attacked, and 42 soldiers and officers were killed on the occasion; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have only a general knowledge of that unfortunate incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You also said yesterday that you had information about Izetbegovic being taken as a hostage while you were away, and I'm telling you now that it was on the 2nd of May. Did you have information, or rather, were you -- was it reported to you -- were you told why Mr. Izetbegovic was taken hostage?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I was, I can't recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: A few days after the briefing that you had with General McKenzie, were you fully aware of the situation or the extent of the problems that existed while these barracks were being evacuated? First of all, did you know how many barracks there were in the town? And then could you also tell me about what you knew about the extent of the problem?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware there were three barracks within the town that remained to be evacuated in mid-May. There was a fourth barracks somewhere out of town which had some officer cadets in it that I was at no time involved with the evacuation of that barracks. And I'm aware that the barracks were invested, surrounded, by the BiH force. And I'm also aware of the difficult circumstances that the JNA faced in extracting their garrisons out of Croatia during the war there and the very hard lessons they learnt there. So I understand the JNA's concern to ensure the safe passage of their soldiers out of the three Sarajevo garrisons, and in particular with their experience in the evacuation, the first one, in early May.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in addition to soldiers and officers there were also members of their families in those barracks, in other words, civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm fully aware of that. And that's one of the reasons that we took every action we possibly could to ensure the safe evacuation of those barracks as a UN force.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So when you arrived on the 14th of May, the situation you found yourself in was that there were hostilities in the town and you described this as happening in the immediate vicinity and sector of Dobrinja. Now, General, sir, could you tell us who held Dobrinja, or rather, I withdraw this question. I apologise. Tell us first: Was Dobrinja a neighbourhood in Sarajevo town itself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This is a neighbourhood that was, we could say, close to the airport; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know what forces held Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time we thought it was a disputed area which changed from time to time, but it was our belief that it was held by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But this balance of power, do you know whether it changed while -- during your stay there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never actually went inside Dobrinja after about the 14th of May, but from reports there was very heavy fighting in there, particularly after the airport agreement. And while there were no big changes of territory there, one side or the other was able to dominate by fire, that's fire-power. But it was always a disputed area during 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
